claims.text: Combining enhanced free-energy sampling with machine-learned interatomic potentials enables prediction of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the HEA family.
The relevant initial materials are multicomponent HEAs in high-temperature solid states approaching melting.
An integrated protocol can combine metadynamics or umbrella sampling with ML-calibrated interatomic potentials for HEAs.
Controlled simulation integration paths near the melting transition are sufficient conditions for applying the proposed protocol.
The free-energy landscape governs the solid-to-liquid transformation.
Enhanced sampling overcomes sampling barriers associated with complex multielement interactions.
Machine-learned potentials provide computational efficiency for simulations of HEA melting.
Machine-learned potentials can capture the intricate energetics of HEA melting.
The integrated method will yield fusion properties aligned with experimental calorimetric measurements.
The method will predict melting temperatures and fusion properties with less than 10% relative error compared with high-temperature experiments.
DSC, high-temperature calorimetry, ab initio calculations, and CALPHAD individually lack either broad HEA applicability or the required efficiency.
Refractory HEAs can have melting points high enough to cause processing difficulties with traditional techniques.
The approach is expected to perform well within the compositional space used to calibrate the ML potentials.
Performance may deteriorate for extreme elemental imbalances or complex phase transitions outside the calibration range.
Transferability of the ML potentials across all HEA compositions is uncertain.
Accuracy may be sensitive to enhanced-sampling window selection and the chosen integration path.

High-temperature calorimetry can directly determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for the validation alloys.
Disagreement exceeding 10% across multiple HEA compositions would falsify the proposed approach.
